composition: The alloy is designated 17Al with the nominal composition Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%). The EDS-measured composition is Fe-43.2, Mn-34.8, Al-17.0 and Cu-5.0 at.%; across the 15Al/17Al/19Al series the nominal Al variation is achieved essentially by substituting Al for Fe while Mn and Cu stay constant. In the design, 35 at.% Mn was chosen to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase, Al is the primary element lowering density (1 wt.% Al reduces density by about 0.1 g/cm3), and Cu was added because it accelerates the aging-hardening response and raises hardness.
conclusions: This 17Al sample represents the high-temperature, long-time aging state of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel study: aging at 650 °C for 10 h converts the α matrix almost fully to β-Mn with 4.7 % of BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates and yields 833.2 ± 18.7 HV at a density of 6.76 g/cm3. Within the 17Al series the 650 °C row is essentially time-independent (about 828–838 HV across 1–10 h) and lies below the alloy's peak hardness, reached at an intermediate temperature (575 °C/6 h, 924.9 HV), showing that the highest hardness of the 17Al alloy is not obtained at the highest aging temperature. In the wider study, Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels with different Al contents were tailored over an ultrawide flexible hardness range of 253.4–965.6 HV through simple short-time aging, and the 15Al alloy achieved an ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm3/g; increasing Al is noted to slow β-Mn precipitation and reduce the toughness of the ultra-hard alloys.
mechanisms: The solution-treated 17Al alloy is single-phase α (BCC); aging drives an α (BCC) → β-Mn transformation in which the α matrix progressively transforms into the Mn-rich β-Mn, and after 10 h at 650 °C this transformation is essentially complete, leaving an equiaxed β-Mn matrix.

The ultra-high hardness of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels originates mainly from the extensive formation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase, whose intrinsic hardness exceeds 10 GPa, so hardness scales with the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn.

β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase, so its nucleation and growth require excluding large amounts of other atoms (including Al) into the surroundings; a higher Al content enriches more Al around the growing β-Mn and also increases and stabilizes the Al-rich D0₃ phase that must first be depleted, so increasing Al slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn and lengthens the time/temperature needed to complete the α→β-Mn transformation.

Rejection of Al from the growing Mn-rich β-Mn enriches Al around the β-Mn interfaces, and this Al enrichment (Al being a BCC stabilizer) promotes the formation of a new fine BCC phase within/at the β-Mn interfaces, as identified by EBSD.

The limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys and the expulsion of Cu from β-Mn during its precipitation and growth cause the formation of an FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces; the amount of this FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces decreases with increasing Al content.

The FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates have intrinsic hardnesses lower than that of β-Mn, so as their quantity increases the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn decreases and the overall hardness falls; the 4.7 % precipitate fraction in this 650 °C/10 h condition is consistent with its hardness lying below the alloy's peak.

Raising the aging temperature accelerates β-Mn precipitation and growth by increasing the driving force for β-Mn formation and the atomic diffusion rate, so the transformation completes rapidly at 650 °C; extended aging beyond the peak allows precipitate growth, making the 650 °C/10 h condition a past-peak, essentially plateau state for the 17Al alloy.
microstructure: After aging at 650 °C for 10 h the α matrix of the 17Al alloy had almost completely transformed into β-Mn. The microstructure consists of an equiaxed β-Mn matrix containing a small amount of new BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates distributed within the β-Mn; the combined volume fraction of the FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates is 4.7 %, and three phases in total are present (β-Mn, BCC, FCC Cu-rich). EBSD (Fig. 5c) shows an equiaxed, randomly oriented grain structure whose phase map is almost pure β-Mn, with the magnified view labelling fine "New BCC phase" particles inside the β-Mn. No grain-size or texture values are reported for this condition.
processing: Ingots of nominal Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%) were produced by vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h and hot-rolled into 4 mm-thick plates, which were cut by electrical discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 specimens. Specimens were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon and oil quenched (the parent process, proc_st-1100c-10min-oq). This sample is the terminal state obtained by subsequently aging the solution-treated material at 650 °C for 10 h followed by water quenching (aging state 650 °C-10h).
properties: Vickers microhardness of the 17Al sample aged at 650 °C for 10 h is 833.2 ± 18.7 HV (HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, 9.8 N load for 15 s, average of 5 measurements on 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 specimens). The alloy density is 6.76 g/cm3, measured by the Archimedes method. Characterization of this sample used EBSD on a GeminiSEM 300 SEM, with a scanning step size of 1.5 μm at low magnification and 0.05 μm at high magnification, performed on electrolytically polished surfaces (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol), together with Vickers microhardness testing. No tensile, fracture-toughness or nanoindentation values are reported for this specific 650 °C/10 h condition.
summary: This is the 17Al (Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu at.%) low-density steel in the terminal state obtained by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min (argon, oil quench) followed by aging at 650 °C for 10 h and water quenching. It belongs to a study of how Al content controls the aging-hardening behaviour of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels, in which the near-complete α→β-Mn transformation is the microstructural origin of the ultra-high hardness.
unmapped: For the 17Al alloy the peak Vickers hardness of the whole aging series was 924.9 ± 25.8 HV, reached at 575 °C for 6 h (Table 3), which is a different aging condition from this 650 °C/10 h sample.

The indentation fracture toughness KIC of the hardest 17Al sample (575 °C/6 h, HV = 924.9) was 6.6 MPa·m1/2, calculated with Eq. (1) using E = 175 GPa for 17Al and an average crack length of 22 μm; this value is reported for the peak-hardness condition, not for the 650 °C/10 h sample.

Nanoindentation of the β-Mn in the hardest 17Al sample (575 °C/6 h) gave an average intrinsic hardness of 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa and an overall H_Ave of 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa, and that β-Mn contained 16.3 at.% Al, 36.2 at.% Mn and 2.6 at.% Cu; these values pertain to the 575 °C/6 h condition rather than to this 650 °C/10 h sample.
